unit.unitOverview: Say what you do every day: I get up at seven. Say what another person does: she works, he studies. Say how often: always, usually, sometimes, never. Say what you are doing now: today I am relaxing. Say what you want, need and prefer.
unit.learningPath:
The lesson: listen and repeat.
Words: listen, look and say. 24 words.
Patterns: 4 cards. Read the one done for you.
Reading: a day, a short report and a notice.
Speaking: tap the mic. Say it. Listen.
Writing: write about your week. Made-up is OK.
Practice: write. Check with the answers.
Quiz: 12 questions. At the end, My progress.

visual.lectureScript:
Hello! This is Unit 14.
In this unit, you talk about every day.
What do you do every day? What does a friend do?
Listen.
I wake up at six. I get up at half past six.
I have a shower and I get dressed.
I have breakfast at seven.
I do these things every day.
For every day, use the doing word as it is.
I work. We start at nine. They travel by bus.
Now listen to he, she and it.
She works in a shop. He studies English. The bus stops here.
With he, she and it, the doing word changes at the end.
work, works. start, starts. travel, travels.
Some words change a little more.
watch, watches. wash, washes. relax, relaxes.
go, goes. do, does.
study, studies. carry, carries.
And have is different: she has lunch at one.
Say the end of each word clearly. She works. He watches TV.
In a question, does has the change, and the doing word does not.
Does she work on Sunday? No, she doesn't. She doesn't work on Sunday.
Now, is it every day, or is it now?
Every day: Dan works in a café.
But today is Sunday.
Now: Dan is not working. He is relaxing at home.
Every day, usually and often go with works.
Now and today go with is working.
Now, how often?
Look at one week.
Always: all seven days.
Usually: five or six days.
Often: three or four days.
Sometimes: one or two days.
Never: no days at all.
The how-often word goes before the doing word.
I always get up at six. She never drinks coffee.
With am, is and are, it goes after.
I am always tired on Monday. The bus is never late.
Every goes with a time: every day, every week, every Saturday.
It comes at the end: I do the shopping every Saturday.
Ask: How often do you cook?
Answer: Every day. Or: Sometimes. Or: Never.
Last, four words you cannot see: want, need, know and prefer.
You can see a person work. You cannot see a person want.
I want a coffee. I need a pen.
I know the answer. Tea or coffee? I prefer tea.
These words do not take -ing, even now.
Say: I want a coffee now. Not: I am wanting a coffee.
After want and need, you can say to: I want to relax.
Mean works the same way: What does weekday mean? It means Monday to Friday.
In Reading, you meet Eva.
What does she do every day? What is she doing today?
Now you. Say three things you do every day.
Put always, usually or never in each one.
Your day can be true or made up.
Now go to Words. Goodbye!

readings.title: Eva's Week, and Eva's Saturday
readings.setting: A person says what she does on weekdays, and what she is doing today.
readings.passageScript:
My name is Eva. On weekdays, I always wake up at six.
I get up at half past six. I have a shower and I get dressed.
I usually have breakfast at seven: bread, an egg and tea.
I study English in the morning. I travel to the library by bus.
In the afternoon, I work at a café near the station.
I have lunch there at two. I never have dinner before eight.
In the evening, I often relax with a book or a film.
But today is Saturday, and I am free!
I am not studying and I am not working.
I am sitting in the park with my brother. We are having lunch in the sun.

readings.setting: A group at a library asks twenty people about their week.
readings.passageScript:
THE LIBRARY WEEK REPORT
Twenty people at the library answered four questions.
1. Do you have breakfast?
14 people always have breakfast. 4 people sometimes have it. 2 people never have it.
2. How do you travel to work or school?
9 people usually travel by bus. 6 people walk every day. 5 people often ride a bike.
3. When do you do the housework?
15 people do it at the weekend. Only 5 people do it on weekdays.
4. What do you want?
18 people want more free time! Only 2 people want more work.

grammar.title: Every day: I work, she works
grammar.explanation:
Use this for things you do every day, or again and again.
I get up at six. We have lunch at one.
With he, she and it, the doing word changes at the end: she works.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
I work in a shop.
You start at nine.
We travel by bus.
They have lunch at one.

He works in a shop.
She starts at nine.
It stops here.

Most words:
work — works
get up — gets up
travel — travels

Ends in ch, sh, x or o:
watch — watches
wash — washes
relax — relaxes
go — goes
do — does

Ends in y:
study — studies
carry — carries
But: play — plays

have — has

After does and doesn't, no change:
Does she work? She doesn't work.
grammar.workedExample:
Eva ___ (watch) TV after dinner.
1. Eva is she.
2. With she, the doing word changes.
3. Watch ends in ch, like wash.
4. It changes a little more: watches.
5. Eva watches TV after dinner.
6. Say it: watches is longer than watch.
grammar.commonMistake:
It is easy to leave the end off after he or she.
No: She work in a shop.
Yes: She works in a shop.
No: He watchs TV.
Yes: He watches TV.
He, she or it at the start? Check the end of the doing word.
grammar.memoryTip: I work. She works. Only he, she and it change.
grammar.practice:
Write the right word.
1. Dan ___ at seven. (get up)
2. I ___ breakfast at home. (have)
3. She ___ TV after dinner. (watch)
4. My brother ___ English. (study)
5. We ___ to work or school by bus. (travel)
6. The film ___ at eight. (start)
7. He ___ the plates after lunch. (wash)
8. Eva ___ lunch at one. (have)
grammar.answerKey:
1. gets up  2. have  3. watches  4. studies  5. travel  6. starts  7. washes  8. has
Wrong on 1? The end goes on get: gets up, not get ups.
Wrong on 2 or 5? I and we: no change.
Wrong on 4? The y goes: studies.
Wrong on 8? Have changes: she has.

grammar.title: Every day or now: I work, I am working
grammar.explanation:
Is it every day, or is it happening now?
Every day: I work in a café.
Now: I am having lunch.
Look for the time words. They tell you which one to use.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Every day:
I work in a café.
She travels by bus.
We usually cook dinner.

Now:
I am working now.
She is travelling by train today.
We are having dinner at a café today.

Words for every day:
every day, usually, often, on Mondays

Words for now:
now, today, Look!

Both in one line:
I usually walk, but today I am taking a taxi.
grammar.workedExample:
Today is Sunday. Dan ___ (not work). He ___ (relax) at home.
1. Today: it is happening now.
2. Use am, is or are, and the -ing word.
3. Dan is not working.
4. He is relaxing at home.
5. Every day he works. Today he is relaxing.
6. Check: is and -ing in both lines. Yes.
grammar.commonMistake:
It is easy to use -ing for every day.
No: Every morning I am having a shower.
Yes: Every morning I have a shower.
It is easy to drop am, is or are.
No: She working now.
Yes: She is working now.
grammar.memoryTip: Every day: I work. Now: I am working.
grammar.practice:
Write the right form.
1. I ___ lunch at one every day. (have)
2. Look! The bus ___. (come)
3. She usually ___ by bus. (travel)
4. Today she ___ by train. (travel)
5. We ___ TV now. (watch)
6. He often ___ dinner. (cook)
7. It is ten o'clock at night. The baby ___ now. (sleep)
8. I ___ on weekdays. (work)
grammar.answerKey:
1. have  2. is coming  3. travels  4. is travelling  5. are watching  6. cooks  7. is sleeping  8. work

grammar.title: How often: always, usually, never
grammar.explanation:
Say how many times you do a thing.
The how-often word goes before the doing word: I always get up at six.
With am, is and are, it goes after: I am always tired.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
In one week:
always: all seven days
usually: five or six days
often: three or four days
sometimes: one or two days
never: no days at all

Before the doing word:
I always get up at six.
She usually has lunch at one.
We never drink coffee.

After am, is and are:
I am often tired on Monday.
The bus is never late.

Sometimes can go first too:
Sometimes I walk to work or school.

Every comes at the end:
I walk to the shop every day.
She does the shopping every week.

How often do you cook?
Every day. Sometimes. Never.
grammar.workedExample:
Make one line: Dan / always / gets up / at six.
1. Find the doing word: gets up.
2. Always goes before it.
3. Dan always gets up at six.
4. Now with is: Dan / always / is / tired.
5. Always goes after is.
6. Dan is always tired.
7. Check: before the doing word, after is. Yes.
grammar.commonMistake:
It is easy to put don't with never.
No: I don't never drink coffee.
Yes: I never drink coffee.
Never is already no.
It is easy to put the word at the end.
No: I get up at six always.
Yes: I always get up at six.
grammar.memoryTip: Before the doing word. After am, is and are.
grammar.practice:

4. He walks to work or school. (sometimes)

6. I drink coffee. (never)
7. I do the shopping. (every Saturday)
grammar.answerKey:
1. I usually get up at seven.
2. She is never late.
3. We often have fish on Friday.
4. He sometimes walks to work or school. Or: Sometimes he walks to work or school.
5. They are always busy on Monday.
6. I never drink coffee.
7. I do the shopping every Saturday.
Wrong on 2 or 5? After is and are: is never, are always.
Wrong on 7? Every Saturday goes at the end.

grammar.title: Want, need, know, prefer: not with -ing
grammar.explanation:
You can see a person work. You cannot see a person want.
Want, need, know and prefer are words like this.
Do not add -ing to them, even now: I want a tea now.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
I want a coffee.
She wants a new phone.
I need a pen.
He needs help.
I know the answer.
She knows my address.
Tea or coffee? I prefer tea.
She prefers the bus.

Now, and still no -ing:
I want a tea now.
Not: I am wanting a tea.

Want to, need to:
I want to relax.
She needs to go home.

Mean is the same:
What does free mean?
It means not busy.
grammar.workedExample:
Choose: I (want / am wanting) a glass of water now.
1. Can you see a person want? No.
2. Want takes no -ing, even now.
3. I want a glass of water now.
4. With she: She wants a glass of water now.
5. Check: no am, no -ing. Yes.
grammar.commonMistake:
It is easy to add -ing when it is now.
No: I am needing a pen now.
Yes: I need a pen now.
It is easy to leave out to after want.
No: I want relax.
Yes: I want to relax.
grammar.memoryTip: You can see work. You cannot see want.

1. need  2. is cooking  3. knows  4. prefer  5. want  6. does  7. are watching
Wrong on 2 or 7? You can see a person cook and watch. Now: is cooking, are watching.
Wrong on 1, 3, 4 or 5? These words take no -ing, even now.
Wrong on 6? Ask with does: What does it mean?

teacherNotes.noteType: The one error worth your attention
teacherNotes.note: The he, she and it ending is the error learners keep making long after they know the rule: she work, he watch. Listen for it in Speaking 2 and look for it in Writing 2. When you hear it, point at the start of the line (she, he, the bus) and let the learner fix the end of the doing word. The second most common error is -ing for a routine: every morning I am having a shower. Point at the time word.

teacherNotes.note: No task assumes a job, a school, a commute, a partner or children. Where a line splits by life stage it says work or school, and every task about the learner's own day says it can be made up. A made-up day practises the language exactly as well as a true one; never ask whether it is real.

teacherNotes.noteType: What is and is not taught here
teacherNotes.note: Questions with do and does, and don't and doesn't, were taught in Unit 7 and are used freely, with no card. The -ing for now was Unit 5; here it is only contrasted with the routine form. The fourth card keeps state verbs to want, need, know, prefer and mean. Leave think, have for owning and similar cases alone: at this level the rule is you can see a person work, you cannot see a person want. Like with -ing (I like cooking) is Unit 4 and is a different pattern from I am liking, which this unit does not mention.
